offset.n: A verb often found in economics and environment essays, usually passive: costs were offset by gains, or companies offset their emissions. It takes a direct object and the preposition by, not with. As a verb the stress is on the second syllable (off-SET), while the noun is stressed on the first (OFF-set). It is more formal than make up for and fits IELTS Writing Task 1 when one trend cancels another. Do not confuse it with compensate, which often needs for.
x: Planting forests may partly offset the carbon released by air travel.
The rise in rent was offset by a small pay increase.
Cheaper imports helped to offset the impact of higher fuel prices.

ongoing.n: Use ongoing before a noun for something that began earlier and is still happening: an ongoing investigation, ongoing negotiations, an ongoing debate. After a linking verb (The talks are ongoing) it is common in news but less so in formal essays, where in progress is safer. It is neutral and a little more formal than continuing, and it does not mean repeated, so a regular habit is not ongoing. Stress falls on the first syllable (ON-going).
x: The ongoing negotiations between the two companies have not yet produced an agreement.
Scientists are involved in an ongoing study of how sleep affects memory.
Staff were reassured that the ongoing repairs would not disturb lessons.

overlap.n: As a verb it is intransitive or takes with: the two courses overlap, or this topic overlaps with another. The noun is stressed on the first syllable (OH-ver-lap), and the verb is often stressed on the last. It describes shared time, space or content, so it is useful for comparing categories in essays. Do not add each other after it, and avoid saying overlap together. The past form is overlapped, with the p doubled before the ending.
x: Our working hours overlap for only two hours each day.
The symptoms of the two illnesses often overlap, which makes diagnosis harder.
Her responsibilities overlap with those of the marketing manager.

overseas.n: It works as an adjective before a noun (overseas students) and as an adverb after a verb (study overseas), and in both uses it has no preposition: write go overseas, not go to overseas. As an adverb it is stressed on the last syllable (oh-ver-SEEZ). It is one word, and the form oversea is rare. It is slightly more formal than abroad, which is the usual everyday adverb (live abroad), and it fits IELTS topics on education, trade and migration.
x: Many graduates look for work overseas after finishing university.
The company opened three overseas offices last year.
Overseas visitors must show their passports at the entrance.

parameter.n: A formal noun that appears in science, computing and project work. Its stress is on the second syllable (puh-RAM-i-ter). In general English it usually appears in the plural, meaning limits or boundaries: within the parameters of the study. Do not confuse it with perimeter, which means the outer edge of an area. In maths and programming it means a variable with a set value. Avoid using it as a fancy word for any factor, because it implies a fixed limit or a measurable value.
x: The teacher explained the parameters of the assignment before we began.
Engineers adjusted the temperature parameter to improve the results.
Within these parameters, there is plenty of room for creative solutions.

perceive.n: A formal verb followed by an object and often as: people perceive the risk as low. The passive be perceived as is very common in IELTS essays about attitudes. Spelling is a frequent problem, since it follows the rule i before e except after c, so write perceive, not percieve. The noun is perception and the adjective is perceptive. It is stronger than see in the sense of understand, and it can also mean to notice through the senses, as in perceive a sound.
x: Younger voters often perceive politicians as out of touch.
Few people perceive the slow change in climate from year to year.
The patient could perceive only light and shadow after the operation.

persist.n: An intransitive verb meaning to continue, usually after a point where it might be expected to stop. With in plus an -ing form, it describes people who keep trying: she persisted in asking questions. Without a preposition, it describes problems, such as fever persists. Stress falls on the second syllable (per-SIST), and the noun is persistence. It is more formal than keep on and has a slightly positive tone for people but a negative one for problems. Do not use it with a direct object.
x: If the pain persists, you should see a doctor.
He persisted in his search for work despite many rejections.
Poverty persists in some rural areas, even in wealthy countries.

philosophy.n: The noun is stressed on the second syllable (fi-LOS-o-fee) and is uncountable when it means the academic subject: she studies philosophy. It is countable when it means a personal or organisation's belief, as in a philosophy of life. Do not confuse it with philosopher, which is the person. Typical partners are moral philosophy, Greek philosophy and a philosophy of education. In business writing it is a slightly grand way to say approach, so use it only for a set of guiding principles.
x: She chose to study philosophy because she enjoys asking big questions.
The company's philosophy is to treat every customer as a friend.
Ancient Greek philosophy still influences modern debates about ethics.

portion.n: A noun meaning a part of a whole, or the amount of food served to one person. A large portion of is typical in IELTS Task 1 descriptions, and it is followed by of plus a noun phrase: a large portion of the population. It is more formal than part and less precise than percentage or proportion. In restaurants it refers to the size of a meal, as in a generous portion. Do not confuse it with proportion, which compares relative size.
x: A small portion of the profits is donated to charity.
The restaurant is known for its generous portions of pasta.
A large portion of the population lives in the capital city.

pose.n: Commonly used in academic collocations: pose a threat, pose a risk, pose a problem and pose a question. In these uses it is formal and means to present something that has to be dealt with. It is a regular verb, so the past form is posed. Pose a question sounds more written and deliberate than ask a question, so it suits essays and reports rather than casual talk. The other meaning is to sit or stand still for a photograph or painting, as in pose for a portrait.
x: Plastic waste poses a serious risk to marine life.
The new technology poses several questions about privacy.
The children posed for a photograph in front of the school.

preliminary.n: An adjective used before a noun, never after be in everyday use, and stressed on the second syllable (pri-LIM-i-nair-ee). It describes steps or findings that come before the main stage: preliminary results, a preliminary report or preliminary talks. It suggests the final outcome is still uncertain, so it is useful in IELTS Writing when discussing research. It is more formal than first or early. As a noun in the plural, preliminaries means introductory steps. Do not confuse it with primary, which means main.
x: The preliminary findings will be published next week.
Preliminary talks between the two leaders took place in Geneva.
After a preliminary check, the inspector allowed the plant to reopen.

priority.n: A countable noun, so write a priority or priorities, not prioritys. The plural is priorities, with the y changed to i. Common patterns are top priority, give priority to, and take priority over. It is stressed on the second syllable (pry-OR-i-tee). It is neutral in tone and widely used in IELTS essays about government spending. The related verb is prioritise (prioritize in American English). In essays, name what comes first and say why, instead of using top priority as an empty phrase.
x: Cutting costs is not our main priority this year.
Emergency patients take priority over routine appointments.
Governments must decide whether education or healthcare should be the higher priority.

psychology.n: The word begins with a silent p, so say sy-KOL-o-jee. It is an uncountable noun when it refers to the subject, and a person who studies it is a psychologist. The adjective is psychological. Do not confuse it with psychiatry, which is the medical branch dealing with mental illness. It can also mean the way a group thinks, as in the psychology of voters. Spelling mistakes are common, especially omitting the p or the h in the middle, so check the whole word.
x: He studied psychology at university before becoming a teacher.
The psychology of shopping explains why shops put sweets by the till.
Advertisers rely on psychology to make products seem more attractive.

radical.n: An adjective that can be positive or negative depending on context: a radical solution may be bold, while a radical group may be extreme. It is stressed on the first syllable (RAD-i-kul) and is usually placed before the noun. Common partners are radical change, radical reform and radical approach. It is stronger than significant, and it suggests a break from the past. As a noun, a radical is a person with extreme political views. In IELTS essays it is a good alternative to dramatic.
x: The school introduced a radical new approach to teaching maths.
Radical reform of the tax system could take years.
Their radical ideas shocked many traditional voters.

ratio.n: A ratio compares two quantities and is written with a colon but said with to: a ratio of three to one (3:1). Use of or between before the figures, as in the ratio of men to women or the ratio between income and rent. It differs from proportion, which compares a part with the whole, and from percentage. Typical partners are a high or low ratio and the student-teacher ratio, which make it useful for IELTS Task 1. Say RAY-shee-oh.
x: The ratio of boys to girls in the class is two to three.
A high staff-to-patient ratio improves the quality of care.
The recipe calls for flour and water in a ratio of two to one.

refine.n: A verb with two main uses: to improve something by small changes, as in refine a theory, and to remove impurities, as in refined oil. It is stressed on the second syllable (ri-FINE). The noun is refinement and a place where oil is purified is a refinery. In academic writing it often takes objects such as method, technique, model or approach. It is more precise than improve because it implies fine adjustments. Do not confuse it with define, which means to state a meaning.
x: Designers will refine the app until it is easy to use.
Crude oil must be refined before it can be used as fuel.
She refined her argument after reading the feedback.

register.n: Register for a course or an event, or register with an organisation such as a clinic or a council. You can also register a car, a birth or a complaint, which sounds official. The noun registration names the process. Do not confuse the verb with the linguistic noun register, meaning the level of formality of language (formal register, casual register), which is useful vocabulary for IELTS Speaking. Both are stressed on the first syllable (REJ-is-ter), and the middle e is easy to misspell.
x: Students can register for the course online until Friday.
You must register your car within fourteen days of buying it.
Parents were asked to register with the local clinic.

regulate.n: Regulate means to control something by rules or laws, as in regulate the industry; the person or body doing it is a regulator, and a regulation is a single rule. It is stronger than monitor, because the rule-makers have real power. In biology it has a non-legal sense: the body regulates its temperature. Typical partners are tightly regulated, strictly regulate and government regulation, all useful in essays about the economy. Stress is on the first syllable (REG-yoo-layt).
x: The government plans to regulate online advertising more tightly.
The body regulates its temperature by sweating.
Banks are regulated to protect customers' savings.

restore.n: A verb meaning to bring back something that existed before, such as order, trust or an old building. Typical collocations are restore confidence, restore power and restore a painting. Stress is on the second syllable (ri-STOR). The noun is restoration. It differs from renew, which means to replace with new, and from repair, which is just fixing a fault. It is formal enough for essays and common in news reports about services returning after a failure.
x: Engineers worked through the night to restore power to the town.
The new manager quickly restored trust within the team.
Experts will restore the damaged painting over two years.

rigid.n: Rigid describes things that cannot bend, such as a rigid frame, and, more often in essays, rules or attitudes that allow no flexibility. In the second sense it is usually negative: rigid schedules, a rigid curriculum. Strict says that someone enforces rules firmly, while inflexible is stronger and more personal than rigid. The noun is rigidity. The g is soft and the stress is on the first syllable (RIJ-id). It is handy in IELTS Writing about education systems or working practices.
x: Rigid schedules can make employees feel stressed and unmotivated.
The box is made of rigid plastic, so it protects the glasses.
He held a rigid view of what children should learn.

select.n: A verb for choosing something carefully, usually from a limited group, and a little more formal than choose. It is stressed on the second syllable (si-LEKT). The noun is selection and the adjective select means exclusive, as in a select group. The passive is common in research writing: participants were selected at random. Typical adverbs are carefully and randomly. On websites it is the word telling users to pick an option. Do not use it for casual decisions such as picking lunch.
x: Applicants are selected on the basis of their test scores.
Please select one answer from the list below.
The committee will select three candidates for interviews.

so-called.n: So-called goes before a noun and tells the reader that the name is doubtful or undeserved: the so-called experts, a so-called friend. It is hyphenated, and quotation marks are unnecessary because the word already signals doubt. Sometimes it is neutral and only introduces a new term (the so-called greenhouse effect), but in argument it usually sounds sceptical, even sarcastic, so use it only when you can justify that tone. Stress is on the first part (SOH-kawld).
x: The so-called luxury hotel turned out to have no hot water.
Many people no longer trust so-called experts on social media.
His so-called friends disappeared when he lost his job.

somewhat.n: Somewhat is an adverb meaning to a limited degree, close to rather or a bit but more formal. It modifies adjectives, comparatives and verbs: somewhat higher, somewhat surprised, differs somewhat. It usually stands before the word it modifies and is not combined with very or too. In IELTS Task 1 it suits small changes (rose somewhat). Write it as one word, never some what, and stress the first syllable (SUM-wot).
x: The second experiment was somewhat more successful than the first.
Prices fell somewhat during the summer months.
I was somewhat surprised by how quickly the project finished.

specify.n: A verb meaning to state exactly, and it is stressed on the first syllable (SPESS-i-fy). It is followed by a noun or a clause: specify the date, specify what is needed. The noun is specification, and specific is the adjective. It is formal and typical of contracts, instructions and reports. The past form is specified, with y changed to i, as in specifies. The difference from mention is that specify requires precision. It does not take a person as its object, so do not say specify me the date.
x: Please specify your dietary requirements when you book.
The rules specify that all entries must be submitted by noon.
The report does not specify how many people were interviewed.
